description: Given an array of positive integers nums, you can traverse from index i to j if gcd(nums[i], nums[j]) > 1. Return true if all pairs of indices can reach each other through such traversals.
examples:
Input: nums = [2,3,6]
Output: true
Explanation: gcd(2,6)=2>1, gcd(3,6)=3>1. All connected via index 2.
intuition: Connect indices that share a prime factor, then BFS from index 0. For each prime, connect later indices to the first index with that factor; this connects the whole group without comparing every pair. Use BFS layers so large inputs do not require repeated array-front removals.
approach: Connect indices that share a prime factor, then BFS from index 0. For each prime, connect later indices to the first index with that factor; this connects the whole group without comparing every pair. Use BFS layers so large inputs do not require repeated array-front removals.
explanation:
1. Two values have gcd greater than 1 exactly when they share a prime factor.
2. For each prime, keep the first index containing it. Connect every later index containing that prime to the first one. A star connects the group without constructing every possible pair.
3. Remove all copies of a factor before continuing; a remaining value greater than 1 is also a prime factor.
4. BFS visits the resulting sparse graph one frontier at a time, marking neighbors before scheduling them.
5. Return whether all indices were visited. A single value (even 1) returns true; a 1 among several values remains isolated.
spaceComplexity: O(n + F) for the sparse graph, factor map, and BFS state
hints: Connect indices that share a prime factor, then BFS from index 0. For each prime, connect later indices to the first index with that factor; this connects the whole group without comparing every pair. Use BFS layers so large inputs do not require repeated array-front removals.
Mark a node when scheduling it so repeated paths cannot schedule it again.
Union-find with path compression speeds up repeated connectivity checks in the version below.

followUp.approach: Factorize each number. Use Union-Find: for each number, union the index with a representative index for each of its prime factors. Check if all indices are in the same component.
followUp.jsWalkthrough:
Example: nums = [2,3,6]
n=3, no 1s.
i=0, num=2: prime 2. primeToIdx[2]=0. (num becomes 1, done)
i=1, num=3: prime 3. primeToIdx[3]=1. (num becomes 1, done)
i=2, num=6: factor 2: primeToIdx has 2->0, union(2,0). primeToIdx[2]=0. num=3. factor 3: primeToIdx has 3->1, union(2,1).
Now 0,1,2 are all connected.
root=find(0). find(1)==root, find(2)==root. Return true
followUp.explanation:
1. For each number, factorize it into prime factors.
2. For each prime factor, union the current index with the first index sharing that prime.
3. This connects all indices that share a common prime factor (directly or transitively).
4. After processing all numbers, check if all indices share one root.
5. Handle edge cases: single element (true), contains 1 (false, since gcd(1,x)=1).

timeComplexityBreakdown.variables: n = numbers; M = largest number; F = total distinct-prime occurrences, counted separately for each number.
timeComplexityBreakdown.note: Path compression without rank gives an amortized log n bound per operation. After the early return for 1, every number has at least one prime factor, so F ≥ n and F log n covers the final root checks.
